question: When did Saul become David's enemy?
summary: 1 Samuel 18:8-9 says Saul began to eye David with suspicion immediately after the women's song crediting David with greater slaughter than Saul — "Saul has slain his thousands and David his ten thousands." 1 Samuel 18:27-29 marks the turn after the foreskin bride-price, when "Saul became David's enemy continually." The text gives two different ignition points for the rivalry within the same chapter.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read 18:8-9 and 18:27-29 not as two rival start-dates but as one escalating hostility — suspicion kindled by the song, then hardened into permanent enmity after the bride-price plot failed.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, the upstream source for this very question, sets the two notices side by side — Saul 'eyed David from that day' after the song (18:9) versus Saul 'became David's enemy continually' after the marriage (18:29) — as two different start-points for the rivalry.

pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill addresses the very tension this row presses, keyed to 1 Samuel 18:29: he reconciles the two notices by reading the earlier eyeing of David as enmity 'by fits ... with some intervals' and the later 'continually' as that same enmity now 'rooted and habituated.' A passage-specific harmonizer surfaced on this row, used in place of Haley, whose coverage of this particular within-chapter timing question could not be confirmed.

link.note: No allowlisted (gotquestions.org / carm.org / defendinginerrancy.com) page was found that engages this specific 18:8-9 vs. 18:27-29 ignition-point question; the allowlisted Saul/David pages located treat only adjacent topics (the evil spirit, the song of the thousands, the 17:55 'who is David' crux), so the optional link is omitted rather than co-opted.

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Saul became David's enemy continually; was every day giving fresh evidence of his enmity against him; before it was by fits, and at certain times, there were some intervals; but now enmity was rooted and habituated, and was constant and continually showing itself.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The strongest harmonizing voice: it expressly distinguishes the earlier intermittent enmity (the eyeing of 18:9, 'by fits ... with some intervals') from the now-permanent enmity of 18:29, dissolving the 'two ignition points' into one escalation.
excerpts.source_note_text:
And Saul was yet the more afraid of David,.... Because the Lord was with him, and his wife loved him; so that he feared he should never be able to accomplish his designs, and that this marriage, which he intended as the means of his ruin, would pave the way for his ascending the throne:
and Saul became David's enemy continually; was every day giving fresh evidence of his enmity against him; before it was by fits, and at certain times, there were some intervals; but now enmity was rooted and habituated, and was constant and continually showing itself.
